newsitem.title: USA: Pilots leave UAL task forces in protest.
newsitem.headline: Pilots leave UAL task forces in protest.

text.p: Pilots for UAL Corp's United Airlines are withdrawing from the company's non-essential task forces and may soon refuse to fly overtime, as a dispute over wage and contract issues drags on, a union spokesman said on Tuesday.
"We're going to have them stand down for a while," said Kevin Dohm, a spokesman for the Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) United Master Executive Council.
The pilots' refusal to participate in non-essential task forces will continue until further notice, Dohm said.
Pilots will continue to serve on essential task forces dealing with air safety and scheduling, Dohm said.

ALPA, which turned down a mid-term wage increase earlier this month, likely will begin refusing to fly overtime, Dohm said. He said many United pilots, because of staff shortages, have been flying overtime at straight-pay rates.
"That's one of the items that pilots will have to decide for themselves," Dohm said. "But I imagine all the overtime flying is going to come to a grinding halt."
In a statement, UAL Chairman Gerald Greenwald said he was "extremely disappointed" by the pilots' actions.

"Regardless of what ALPA has been saying, it's clear that the issues raised by the ALPA (Master Executive Council) fundamentally are not about United's culture," Greenwald said. "Instead, they focus on money and their post-ESOP compensation."
Under an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) put in place over two years ago, the pilots, machinists and salaried employees own a majority of UAL Corp.
"Nevertheless, these issues are legitimate and important and deserve -- and will receive -- our priority attention," Greenwald said.

Dohm added that ALPA is having a contract audit conducted to quantify the amount of "contribution" the pilots have made to the airline's bottom line. He said pilots have helped contribute to UAL financial performance by agreeing to fly overtime, deferring vacation and not taking sick time.
"We will present those numbers to the company," Dohm said.
Earlier this month, ALPA rejected United's wage offer with 80 percent voting against a tentative accord. The wage issue now goes to binding arbitration, which must be completed by April 30.
Dohm said all further communication between ALPA and UAL management will be conducted only by Michael Glawe, head of the ALPA United Master Executive Council, and Greenwald.
"I am already talking regularly and directly with...Glawe about ways we can bridge our differences," Greenwald said.
Earlier, UAL reported record fourth quarter earnings on a fully distributed basis of $1.06 a share before charges, up from $0.63 a year ago.
